notes.1a: Almost all candidates recorded the balance readings in the spaces allocated. A high proportion of candidates in some centres did not give thermometer readings to the expected .0 or .5°C and a significant number did not record the initial temperature of FA 1 i.e. temperature at time = 0. Although a variety of temperature rises were recorded many candidates’ temperature changes were sufficiently close to the supervisor’s for credit for accuracy to be awarded.
notes.1i: Many candidates correctly calculated the volume of hydrochloric acid but a number omitted or incorrectly used the mole ratio involved.
notes.1ii: Many candidates gave a correct temperature rise. Some gave the maximum temperature from the instructions. These were usually from the temperature at time = 2 minutes to the maximum temperature.
notes.1c: Answers were generally expected to be given to two to four significant figures.
notes.1iii: Many candidates recognised that it was necessary to divide by 27000 and then multiply by 106.
notes.1d: A large number of candidates correctly stated that they had assumed that the impurity did not react with hydrochloric acid. A significant minority merely commented on the relative amounts of sodium carbonate and impurity.
notes.1e: Many candidates correctly recorded the relevant data and obtained experimental results that demonstrated that they had completed the practical exercise accurately.
notes.1f: Some candidates structured their calculations well to receive full credit.
notes.1g: A number of candidates correctly ticked the first box. Better performing candidates explained their choice in terms of the significance of using a cooling curve.
notes.1h: A significant minority of candidates realised that fewer moles of carbonate were used. Better performing candidates went on to explain the effect of this on the value of ∆H. It was insufficient merely to say that the value was smaller or larger, since this did not make clear the direction of change for a negative value.
notes.2i: It was necessary to note both the effervescence and the formation of a blue/green solution in the first test and then the blue precipitate and its dissolution in excess ammonia to give a dark blue solution.
notes.2ii: Candidates generally were more successful in this part, with only the test with sodium hydroxide and aluminium really producing any significant difficulties. In this test, the ammonia is only produced after the aluminium has been added.
notes.2b: It was evident that many candidates carried out the practical correctly; however credit was not always awarded as not all observations were recorded.
notes.2iii: Where correct observations were recorded, most candidates were able to use this information to identify the cations.
notes.2v: Better performing candidates realised the significance of the difference between anions that were present in FA 5 and anions that could be present. CHEMISTRY
notes.key_messages: • Candidates should avoid the early rounding of intermediate answers during calculations. • Candidates are reminded that observations for a chemical reaction should focus on the physical changes that take place. • The use of the Data Booklet should be encouraged for questions involving infra-red spectra. • When a question asks for a name of a reagent(s) then the formula of reagent(s) is not acceptable. General comments
notes.general_comments: General comments The majority of candidates were able to finish the paper within the hour allowed. Questions 1, 21, 30, 34 and 39 were found to be more challenging to candidates. Comments on specific question The most commonly chosen incorrect answer was C. From the Data Booklet the element is gallium. When three electrons have been removed, the electronic configuration of the Ga3+ ion is 1s22s22p63s23p63d10. The third shell is full at this point.
